**Lemma 2.** _Each graph G generated by the above process_ \(\mathsf{RanG}(\cdot,n)\) _has optimal welfare_ \(\mathrm{OPT}(G)\ge\frac{7n}{8}\) .

_Proof._ Given the fixed ordering over the vertices in _V_ , match each of its first \((1-\frac{1}{8\rho})n\) vertices to its unique neighbor in _W_<sub>2</sub>. Since \(\rho\ge 1\), this gives a matching with welfare at least \(\left(1-\frac{1}{8\rho}\right)n\ge\frac{7n}{8}\) .

_Proof of Theorem 1._ Let \(\Pi\) be a coordination protocol with coordination complexity \(\ell\) and approximation ratio \(\rho\). This means that on a graph instance generated by RanG, the parties can coordinate on a matching with expected weight at least \(\frac{7n}{8\rho}\). Since \(|W_1|=\frac{n}{8\rho}\), we know in expectation at least \(\frac{7n}{8\rho}-\frac{n}{8\rho}=\frac{3n}{4\rho}\) of the vertices in _W_<sub>2</sub> are matched. Let \(\alpha_v\) be the probability that in \(\Pi\), agent _v_ picks her neighbor in _W_<sub>2</sub>. Then, by linearity of expectation, \(\sum_{v\in V}\alpha_v\ge\frac{3n}{4}\) , that is, \(\mathbb{E}_{v\in V}[\alpha_v]\ge\frac{3}{4}\). Hence, there must be some block _B<sub>j</sub>_ such that \(\mathbb{E}_{v\in B_j}[\alpha_v]\ge\frac{3}{4}\). We will now restrict attention to the block _B<sub>j</sub>_ and consider the following instance of **MULTIPLE-INDEX**: for each \(v\in B_j\), set _S<sub>v</sub>=N(v_)--the neighborhood of vertex _v_, and let _u<sub>v</sub>_ be the vertex unique vertex in \(S_v\cap W_2\). Since the message broadcast by the coordination protocol allows the players to identify the special element with average success probability of \(\frac{3}{4\rho}\), by Lemma 1 the length of message

\(\ell\ge(8\mathrm{log}e)|B_j|\left(\frac{3}{4\rho}-\frac{1}{2\rho+1}\right)^2\)<br>
\(\ge(8\mathrm{log}e)\left(\frac{n}{16\rho^2}\right)\left(\frac{3}{4\rho}-\frac{1}{2\rho+1}\right)^2\ge\Omega\left(\frac{n}{\rho^4}\right),\)

which completes the proof.

## 3.3 Lower Bound for Many-to-One Matchings

Finally, we give the following lower bound on coordination complexity for many-to-one matchings. The lower bound relies on the result from Section 3.2--we show that any coordination protocol for many-to-one matchings can also be reduced to a protocol for one-to-one matchings, and so the lower bound in Section 3.2 can be extended to give a lower bound for the many-to-one setting.

For our lower bound instance, we consider bipartite graphs _G_=(_V,E_) such that the vertices in _V_ represent _n_ different players and _W_ represent a set of _k_ goods _j_, each with a supply _b_.

**Theorem 2.** _Suppose that there exists a coordination protocol for many-to-one matchings that guarantees an approximation ratio of_ \(\rho\) _in expectation. Then such a protocol has coordination complexity of_ \(\Omega(k/\rho^4)\).

We will start by considering a one-to-one matching instance generated by RanG with _k_ vertices on each side of the graph \(G'=(V',W',E')\). By Lemma 2, the optimal matching of \(G'\) has size \(\mathrm{OPT}'\ge\frac{7k}{8}\) .

Now we will turn this into an instance of a many-to-one matching problem: make _b_ copies of each vertex in \(V'\) to obtain vertex set _V_ , and set \(W:=W'\) such that the supply of each good _j_ is _b_; then for an edge \((v',w')\) in the original graph, connect all copies of \(v'\) to \(w'\) in the new graph. This gives a bipartite graph _G_=(_V,W,E_). The following claim is straightforward.

**Claim 1.** _The new graph G has a matching of size at least_ \((b\mathrm{OPT}')\).

Now suppose that we could coordinate the players in _V_ to obtain a matching _M_<sup>∗</sup> of size \(\frac{b\mathrm{OPT}'}{\rho}\) in _G_. Then with a simple sampling procedure, we can extract a high cardinality matching for the original graph: for each vertex in \(v'\in V'\), sample one of the _b_ copies of \(v'\) in _G_ uniformly at random along with its incident matched edge. If two vertices in \(V'\) are connected to the same type of good in \(W'\), break ties arbitrarily and keep only one of the edges.
